passage:
Sports day. Worst day.
I was sure I would win the 100 metres. I practised every evening in the colony with Appa timing me. Then the whistle went and Sarika was already ahead, and I could see her plait bouncing the whole way. I came third. THIRD.
My face went so hot. Everybody was clapping for her and I felt the tears coming, so I ran to the girls' toilet and stayed there till the relay was over.
I told Meenal the whistle was late for our side. It WAS late, I think. Maybe.
Appa asked in the car and I said I don't want to talk. I didn't eat the laddoo Amma kept for me 😢
I'm never running again.
— Lavanya

qa.q: Where did Lavanya go when she felt the tears coming?
qa.a: She ran to the girls' toilet and stayed there till the relay was over.

qa.q: How can you tell how hurt and upset Lavanya felt?
qa.a: Her face went hot, she hid until the relay was over, she refused to talk and even skipped the laddoo.

qa.q: How could Lavanya's Appa or Amma help her at this early moment?
qa.a: They could sit with Lavanya, say it's okay to feel upset, and not argue about the whistle yet, so Lavanya feels safe to cry and talk later.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt if she heard Lavanya blame the whistle?
qa.a: Sarika might feel hurt or confused, as if her win was being called unfair.

grounding: It shows a child losing a race, feeling heat in the face and tears, then hiding and blaming the whistle.

passage:
The list went up on the notice board outside the headmaster's room just as the school bell rang for lunch. Tanuja pushed through the crowd of girls, searching for her name under 'Kho-kho: block tournament'. It wasn't there. Zeenat's was.
Her ears burned. Her eyes filled so fast she had to look at the floor. Zeenat turned to say something and Tanuja walked straight past her, out behind the grain shed where the goats were tied, and sat on an upturned bucket.
When her friend Rukhsana found her, Tanuja's voice came out rough. 'Sir always picks his favourites. Zeenat's father helps with the midday meal, that's why.'
She knew it wasn't really why. Zeenat was quicker. But saying it made the lump in her throat a little smaller.
From the field came the shouts of the others practising.

qa.q: Whose name was on the kho-kho list instead of Tanuja's?
qa.a: Zeenat's name was on the list.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja blame the teacher even though she knew Zeenat was quicker?
qa.a: Blaming the teacher made the hurt of being dropped a little easier to bear for the moment.

qa.q: How could Rukhsana support Tanuja right now?
qa.a: She could sit with her and let her be upset without arguing, then later, when Tanuja is calmer, talk about what she wants to work on.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat when Tanuja walks straight past her?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel her good news is spoiled and worry that she has lost a friend over the team list.

grounding: It shows a child dropped from the team, with burning ears and tears, who hides and blames the teacher for picking favourites.

passage:
The whistle went and Keerthana ran harder than she had ever run across the school ground in Hyderabad. For forty metres she was ahead. Then Alka's blue shoes flashed past her, and then two more pairs.
Fourth. Not even a certificate.
Her face went hot, right up to her ears. She felt tears coming and turned towards the wall so nobody would see. When the PT teacher came over with a water bottle, Keerthana said loudly, "The whistle was late for my lane. It's not fair."
The teacher looked at her kindly and didn't argue. Keerthana pulled her cap down low and sat behind the water tank until the next race began, picking at the grass.

qa.q: Which place did Keerthana come in the race?
qa.a: Fourth. Not even a certificate.

qa.q: What does Keerthana turning towards the wall suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, and didn't want anyone to see her tears.

qa.q: What could an adult do at this moment to help Keerthana?
qa.a: Sit with her quietly, say that losing hurts and it's okay to cry, and leave talk about the whistle for later.

qa.q: How might Alka see Keerthana's claim about the whistle?
qa.a: Alka might feel confused or a little hurt, since a fair win now sounds like it was the whistle's doing.

grounding: A child loses a race, feels her face burn and tears come, and her first instinct is to hide and blame the whistle.

passage:
"Pradeep, dinner!" Urmila called. "Why is your door shut?"
"I'm not hungry."
"You're always hungry. Open up."
"..."
"What's that behind your back?"
"Nothing."
"Pradeep."
"It's the maths test. Twelve out of forty. Happy now, didi?"
"Why are you shouting at me?"
"Because the teacher cuts marks for every tiny step! Everyone says she's unfair."
"Your eyes are all red."
"It's the fan. Dust."
"You studied all Sunday. I saw you."
"That's what makes it worse!" His voice cracked. "Don't tell Amma. Please. I'll keep it in my bag till she forgets."

qa.q: What mark did Pradeep get on the maths test?
qa.a: Twelve out of forty.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's claim about dust suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was hurt and ashamed about crying, and didn't want his sister to see how much the mark stung.

qa.q: How could Urmila help Pradeep right now?
qa.a: Sit with him, say it's okay to feel upset after studying so hard, and offer to tell Amma together instead of hiding the paper.

qa.q: What is it like for Urmila to see Pradeep like this?
qa.a: Urmila is worried and a bit stung by his shouting, but sees he is hurting, since she watched him study all Sunday.

grounding: A child who failed a test feels the sting in tears, blames the teacher and wants to hide the paper.

passage:
Last Friday Coach pinned the team list on the notice board. I read it three times. My name wasn't there. Siddharth's was, in my old place, left wing.
My face went burning hot. Tears were coming, and I hated that, because the whole class was standing right there. So I laughed and said, "Whatever, Coach only picks favourites." Siddharth heard and looked at his shoes.
I walked to the washroom fast and stayed there till the bell, splashing water on my face so nobody would know.
I'm Mohit, and I still don't like thinking about that Friday. But I know Siddharth didn't do anything wrong.

qa.q: Which position was Siddharth given on the list?
qa.a: Left wing, Mohit's old place.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when the name wasn't on the list?
qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and humiliated, fighting back tears in front of the whole class.

qa.q: What could Coach or a friend have done that day to help Mohit?
qa.a: Talk with Mohit privately, say that being dropped hurts, and explain what to work on to get back in the team.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt hearing the remark about favourites?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt awkward and a bit hurt, as if the place were unfair, even though Siddharth did nothing wrong.

grounding: A child dropped from the team feels heat in the face and tears, hides in the washroom and blames the coach.

passage:
Coach's note, inter-house sports day, Class 5.
Aparna came fourth in the 100-metre race today, after winning it last year. She crossed the line, went red in the face and walked straight past her house tent to the back of the water tank. When I found her, her eyes were full, and she said, "The whistle was late for our lane. It's not fair." I didn't argue about the whistle. I sat down on the step nearby and said, "That really stings, doesn't it?" She nodded and cried properly then. After a few minutes she let me walk her back. I have told her class teacher, and I will talk with her on Monday about the race, when it hurts less.
Bhupen

qa.q: Where did Aparna go after crossing the line?
qa.a: To the back of the water tank, past her house tent.

qa.q: Why did Aparna blame the whistle?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed at coming fourth after winning last year, and blaming the whistle was easier than facing the sting.

qa.q: How did the coach help Aparna in the moment?
qa.a: The coach did not argue about the whistle, named the sting and sat nearby, which let her cry and then come back.

qa.q: How might Aparna's class teacher help after hearing from the coach?
qa.a: The class teacher could keep a gentle eye on Aparna and offer a kind word, so the sting is not faced alone.

grounding: Shows a child losing a race, going red and teary, and first wanting to hide and blame the whistle.
